0.body: English | 中文 Agent2App is an umbrella term for cases where an Agent returns more than text and hands some form of application capability to a Host. There are two product tracks under that umbrella, and they must stay separate: agent2view: the Agent generates or declares a live app view inside an existing Host . The Host owns rendering, state boundaries, permission boundaries, and action dispatch. aichat inline runsplash UI, Robrix2 Matrix app-cards, and Mission Room all belong to this track. agent2project: the Agent generates an independent project or application artifact . The output is no longer an in-host live view; it is a file tree, resources, crate/package metadata, state modules, event handler code, and run/export/package targets. flowchart TB A[Agent2App] A --> V[agent2view: runtime app view] A --> P[agent2project: generated project artifact] V --> C[aichat inline AppGen] V --> R[Robrix2 Matrix app-card] V --> M[Mission Room] P -. future .-> F[files / resources / crate / run targets] This little book defines agent2view: the protocol where an Agent produces an app view and the Host safely renders it while enforcing state and action boundaries. agent2project needs a separate artifact protocol and must not reuse the agent2view capability manifest as-is. The central revision in this edition is that agent2view first defines a shared protocol kernel , then defines transport bindings, view encodings, and application scenarios. Remote Agents and local Agents use the same kernel semantics; they differ only in message carrying, permission boundaries, state submission paths, and Host profiles. flowchart TB K[Agent2View Core Kernel] K --> B[Transport Binding] B --> L[Local Binding] B --> R[Remote / Event Binding] K --> E[View Encoding] E --> S[Makepad runsplash] E --> U[A2UI message bundle] K --> P[Application Profiles] P --> A[aichat AppGen Scenario] P --> X[Robrix2 IM App-Card Scenario] X --> M[Mission Room Scenario] How to read this book Read Part I for the protocol core. It defines the object model, state model, and action semantics shared by local and remote Agents. Read Part II for the current Host profiles. aichat and Robrix2 are application scenarios built on top of the shared kernel. Read Part III for safety, versioning, and validation.
0.title: Preface

1.body: The core goal of Agent2App is to define how an Agent hands a structured app view to a Host for rendering, and how user operations inside that view return to the Host or Agent. This specification currently covers only agent2view.

104.body: The discussions expand Agent2App from an aichat demo into three mutually reinforcing engineering tracks: Local AppGen: aichat generates inline runsplash views Room AppGen: Robrix/Matrix hosts shared, persistent, collaborative app views Software Factory: component skills, Host APIs, test harnesses, and model evaluation loops produce working apps The shared conclusion is that Makepad should not be framed only as a Skia replacement or a Flutter-like UI toolkit. The stronger story is that Makepad + Robius + Splash can become a cross-platform native app runtime for the AI era. Splash is not meant to replace Rust for every piece of logic; it gives AI a low-token, streamable, recoverable, Host-embeddable executable template language. flowchart TB Core[Agent2App Core Kernel] Core --> Local[aichat Local AppGen] Core --> Room[Robrix Matrix Room App] Core --> Factory[AI App Software Factory] Local --> RS[runsplash inline view] Local --> HS[Host-owned data/state] Local --> API[Splash Host API] Room --> MX[Matrix event/state binding] Room --> Shared[shared room data] Room --> Personal[personalized view per user] Factory --> Skills[component skills] Factory --> Harness[model-specific harness] Factory --> Tests[headless/remote UI tests]
104.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Discussion Synthesis: Makepad/Splash Agent2App Roadmap
104.title: Discussion Synthesis: Makepad/Splash Agent2App Roadmap

105.body: Traditional frameworks assume that the primary author is a human. Agent2App assumes that the primary generator is a model, which changes the constraints: model context windows are limited; model capability varies widely; models have little Splash training data; generating UI and generating reliable app logic have different difficulty profiles; generating a full Rust/HTML/JS app in one shot can work, but it is slow, expensive in tokens, and exposes a larger error surface. The goal for Splash should therefore be: the lowest-token executable app representation The model generates a shorter Splash template, the Host provides data/state/action/API boundaries, and the runtime plus test harness handle reliability.
105.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » AI-native Runtime, Not a Traditional Framework
105.title: AI-native Runtime, Not a Traditional Framework

106.body:
The recurring term in the discussions is harness. Here, harness means more than a prompt. It is a dynamically selected constraint package based on model, target device, AppType, available components, and error feedback: model capability
target device
AppType
component skills
Host API manifest
runtime error feedback
test result -> selected harness/context Strong frontier models can be allowed to generate more original structure. Smaller or local models should be constrained by stronger templates, fixed components, and less freedom. For weak models, the recommended path is not to create a complete app from scratch, but to: select components
fill configuration
generate a small delta
call Host APIs This reduces creativity but improves usability. The baseline should be reliability and usefulness; advanced visual effects can be enabled according to model ability, time budget, and device capability.

106.title: Harness Strength Should Vary by Model and Target

107.body: If the model regenerates calendar, todo, weather, poll, trip planner, or mission room widgets from scratch every time, context grows and quality becomes unstable. A better shape is: App request -> semantic routing -> load relevant component skills -> model emits config/delta -> Host/Splash runtime composes final view Candidate component skills include: Todo / collection Calculator Timer Calendar / agenda Poll Trip planner Barcamp scheduler Mission room Dashboard / -1 screen card A component skill can include Splash snippets, Host API wrappers, schema, examples, and test fixtures. Longer term, the project can generate and publish a large Splash example corpus so future models, LoRA adapters, or retrieval contexts can learn Splash more reliably.
107.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Component Skills Are Reusable Assets
107.title: Component Skills Are Reusable Assets

108.body:
Generated apps are transient. If business state lives inside a Splash widget instance, it can be lost when the timeline scrolls, the widget is recycled, or the view is regenerated. The correct boundary is: Host / Matrix room owns data and shared truth
HostState owns local draft and view state
Splash owns the current view template
Widget instance owns only transient rendering state This means PortalList or timeline recycling is not a protocol problem. Visible widgets may be freed; AppInstance, DataSnapshot, and HostState must live at a higher layer.
108.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » State Owner Must Be Host or Room, Not Generated Widget
108.title: State Owner Must Be Host or Room, Not Generated Widget

109.body: Matrix already has a widget concept, but the current shape is closer to iframe/webview apps. It can access room state and support collaborative examples such as schedules, but it is heavy, client support is expensive, and ecosystem usage is low. Robrix + Splash can provide a lighter native room app binding: Matrix room event / room state -> Robrix validates org.octos.app envelope -> Robrix creates AppInstance -> injects scoped room data into Splash VM -> renders Splash view inline in room -> user action goes through Host API -> producer writes Matrix event/state update -> all clients re-project data into their own view sequenceDiagram participant A as Agent participant M as Matrix Room participant R as Robrix Host participant VM as Splash VM participant U as User participant P as Producer A->>M: org.octos.app + Splash template R->>M: read room event/state R->>R: validate AppType, scope, capabilities R->>VM: inject room data projection + Host API VM->>U: render inline room app U->>VM: click/type/drag VM->>R: app.action(...) R->>R: validate action and payload R->>P: submit shared action P->>M: new DataSnapshot/action event R->>VM: refresh projected data This supports two important capabilities: multiple room members can collaborate on the same shared data; each user can render the same data through their own view/template. For example, a family trip planner can share itinerary, participants, and tasks while each member uses a different layout: calendar view, map-first view, task list, or compact card. Matrix is a transport binding, not the protocol kernel. The Agent2App kernel still defines AppInstance, DataSnapshot, Template, Action, Scope, and Permission. Matrix binding decides how to encode those concepts into room events, room state, or widget-like events.
109.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Robrix/Matrix: From Webview Widgets to Splash Room Apps
109.title: Robrix/Matrix: From Webview Widgets to Splash Room Apps

11.body: AppInstance is a concrete running entity of an AppType under a specific scope. It is not the same as a single message. A room scoped app can be rendered by multiple messages and point to the same instance.
11.title: AppInstance

110.body:
One concrete landing point is that Splash script can be part of room content instead of an external app package. Example shape: { "org.octos.app": { "type": "room_poll", "version": 1, "scope": "room", "app_id": "poll.dinner", "data": {}, "template": { "format": "splash", "code": "RoundedView{ ... }" }, "capabilities": ["app.action", "app.collection"] }
} This lets Robrix treat Agent-generated views as rich interactive chat/room content, not as separately installed applications.

110.title: Matrix Splash App as a Room Artifact

111.body:
The later discussion moves toward a software factory. The goal is not to manually fix a calculator demo, but to build a repeatable pipeline: App spec
component skills
model-specific harness
generated Splash/Rust artifact
headless or remote UI run
virtual click/type/scroll
state/action assertions
runtime errors -> feedback into harness flowchart LR Spec[App spec] --> Ctx[model harness/context] Ctx --> Gen[generate Splash/app artifact] Gen --> Run[run in headless or remote Host] Run --> Act[virtual click/type/scroll] Act --> Assert[state/action assertions] Assert -->|pass| Keep[accept harness/app] Assert -->|fail| Err[collect runtime errors] Err --> Tune[mutate context or component skill] Tune --> Gen This moves Agent2App from "can the model draw UI" to "can the model produce a working app". The test target must go beyond parse/render: button clicks must emit the correct action; input must preserve focus and draft state; collection add/toggle/delete must change Host data; calculator operator/equal/clear must be correct; timer start/pause/reset must be correct; state template refresh must not rewrite input source on every keypress. Makepad-native widgets can use a unified automation path. Platform-native widgets need per-platform adapters because iOS, macOS, Android, and WebView differ in lifecycle, query, event injection, and compositing behavior.
111.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Software Factory: From Demo to Verified Production Line
111.title: Software Factory: From Demo to Verified Production Line

112.body: The current simple streaming eval strategy keeps trying to evaluate, ignores errors, and retries until the code becomes complete. This works, but it is noisy and can enter unrecoverable states. Hardening directions: evaluate only on complete scope/block boundaries; incomplete scopes must not create fatal state; infinite loops, timeout, and memory overuse must be interruptible; VM errors must be returned structurally to the harness; the streaming parser should identify complete widgets, complete let bindings, and complete callbacks; repeated eval should reuse stable parts where possible to reduce flicker and focus loss. These are not kernel requirements, but they are runtime quality gates for the aichat and Robrix profiles.
112.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Splash Streaming Eval and VM Hardening
112.title: Splash Streaming Eval and VM Hardening

113.body: Makepad can wrap native components and can also provide Makepad-native widgets. These two paths have different boundaries. On Apple platforms, native component contents often cannot be read by the application and then warped by a custom shader glass effect. The system compositor protects content such as Safari or banking views. Apps can overlay transparent content, but readback-based refraction or blur generally requires the Apple system compositor or screen capture permission. Profiles should therefore distinguish: Makepad-native widget: cross-platform rendering, unified testing, Makepad shader/glass/vector effects Platform-native component: system capability reuse, but testing, compositing, and permissions are per-platform Everything React Native can wrap, Makepad/Robius can in principle wrap too; glass, readback, snapshot, and automation need platform-specific handling.
113.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Native Components and Platform Compositing Boundaries
113.title: Native Components and Platform Compositing Boundaries

114.body: The discussions also compare SVG, Splash vector drawing, and shaders. The conclusion is not that Agent2App must generate SVG: small animated UI elements, icons, arrows, and micro interactions fit shaders; large complex graphics should not abuse shaders; complex shapes such as a tiger or logo are better handled by vector/raster pipelines; Splash can expose a Makepad-native vector/shader DSL that is simpler than SVG for generated UI; standardized SVG is optional if the target runtime has a concise, stable native expression. This supports a broader principle: Agent2App Template should not be bound to Web/SVG encoding. Makepad-native template encoding is a first-class path.
114.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Vector, SVG, and Shader Boundaries
114.title: Vector, SVG, and Shader Boundaries

115.body:
The discussions form a cautious reading of Apple policy: the risk is not interpretation itself, but whether the app lets users download, generate, and execute new code that changes app functionality after review. High-risk framing: Generate any app
AI app store
Run arbitrary downloaded applications
Replace App Store Lower-risk framing: AI chat with rich interactive content
Room-native collaborative widgets
Configurable mini apps inside a declared Host
Predeclared calendar/poll/collection/dashboard capabilities Product language should emphasize agent2view, not agent2project. The Host's primary purpose should be declared as chat, collaboration, or room interaction. Splash/A2UI views are rich content under that purpose, not a general-purpose app store replacement. Android and Web/WASM can be more aggressive. iOS App Store builds should prefer predeclared capabilities and configurable widgets. TestFlight, Web demos, Android sideload, and desktop builds can be used as freer experimentation channels.
115.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Distribution and App Store Boundary
115.title: Distribution and App Store Boundary

116.body: Phase 0: Local AppGen aichat reliably generates runsplash views with Host API, state projection, and basic actions. Phase 1: Host API app.action / app.input / app.collection / ai.talk replace direct public use of agent.notify. Phase 2: Verification Harness calculator, todo, timer, poll, and calendar enter the automated headless/remote test suite. Phase 3: Component Skills common mini apps become component skill + schema + examples + tests. Phase 4: Robrix Room App Matrix events carry app envelopes and Splash templates; Robrix renders them inline. Phase 5: Shared Collaboration actions write back to Matrix events/state; users share data while keeping personalized views. Phase 6: Distribution Strategy Web/WASM and Android show the full dynamic runtime first; iOS uses rich chat content with predeclared capabilities.
116.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Recommended Milestones
116.title: Recommended Milestones

117.body: Final naming for Splash Host API: app.*, host.*, or profile-specific namespace. Matrix room app event schema: template in event content, room state, or both. AppInstance lifecycle: timeline visibility, room membership, permission changes, history restore. VM resource limits: CPU, memory, timer, network, file, native API. Component skills packaging: plain text, repo artifact, Matrix event, or Host-bundled library. Minimum app suite and scoring rules for per-model harness eval. App Store wording and product capability boundaries. These issues do not block the current protocol kernel, but they decide the product path for aichat and Robrix profiles.
117.breadcrumbs: Appendix: JSON Examples, Binding Evolution, and Discussion Synthesis » Open Decisions
117.title: Open Decisions

12.body: ScopeKey is the stable identity of an AppInstance. flowchart TB S{scope} S --> M[message] S --> R[room] S --> A[account] M --> MK["room_id + event_id"] R --> RK["room_id + app_id"] A --> AK["account_id + app_id"] A local scenario can map room_id to a local workspace or session id; a remote scenario can directly use Matrix room/account/event ids. The mapping differs, but ScopeKey semantics do not.
12.title: ScopeKey

13.body: ViewSpec is the view description the Agent wants the Host to render. ViewSpec contains at least: AppType; ScopeKey; Template or template id; State binding; Capability manifest; list of triggerable actions. aichat can encode ViewSpec as appplan json + runsplash. Robrix2 can encode ViewSpec as an org.octos.app envelope + local template id.
13.title: ViewSpec

14.body: Snapshot is the authoritative state snapshot of an AppInstance. In a local Agent scenario, Snapshot can be maintained by HostState and projected into the view on every render. In a remote Agent scenario, Snapshot is usually written by a remote producer into a shared event log such as a Matrix timeline. Regardless of source, Snapshot must satisfy the AppType state schema.
14.title: Snapshot

15.body: Template is the description that renders state into UI. The protocol kernel only requires Template to be preflightable by the Host and bindable to state. It does not require Template to be generated by an LLM or to be locally static. The concrete profile decides the Template source: the aichat profile allows LLM-generated runsplash, but it must be constrained by a capability manifest; the Robrix2 v1 profile allows only local static .splash templates and does not allow Matrix events or LLMs to directly provide runtime templates.
15.title: Template

16.body: Action is the intent emitted by the user or view. There are two Action categories: Local View Action: affects only the current local view/session. Shared Fact Action: changes shared facts and must be validated by an Agent/producer before producing a new Snapshot. The Action type is determined by the AppType action schema and profile policy, not by the transport. agent.notify can carry local actions; org.octos.action_response can carry shared actions; future transports should carry the same Action semantics.
16.title: Action

17.body: Transport binding maps the shared protocol kernel to concrete message carriers. It does not change protocol semantics. It only changes how data is transmitted, who can observe it, and how failure degrades.
17.title: Transport Binding

18.body: Core Concept Local Binding Remote/Event Binding AgentEndpoint current LLM session / local tool Agent Matrix room Agent / server-side producer ViewSpec appplan json + runsplash org.octos.app envelope + template id Snapshot HostState / APP_DEMO_STATE Matrix event content Template LLM-generated runsplash or local template locally registered static template Action agent.notify(event_id, payload) org.octos.action_response ActionResult Host local reducer result new snapshot event produced by Agent Failure log/ignore or show error view fall back to body
18.title: Kernel-to-Binding Mapping

19.body: Local binding is used by local AppGen scenarios such as aichat. sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant A as Local AgentEndpoint participant H as Host participant M as Markdown/Splash participant S as HostState U->>H: prompt H->>A: prompt + current snapshot/capability A-->>H: ViewSpec(appplan + runsplash) H->>M: render template with HostState U->>M: click / type M->>H: Action via agent.notify H->>S: validate + reduce H->>M: re-render visible views Characteristics: The Agent and Host are in the same local interaction loop. The Host owns the current Agent session. The Host can directly maintain HostState. The Host can immediately handle local actions and update UI. agent.notify is the reverse channel of the local binding, not the shared protocol kernel itself.
19.title: Local Binding

2.body: agent2view must solve five problems: How an Agent declares the app view it wants rendered. How the Host validates app type, state, template, and action. How the Host stores state so authoritative state is not lost when widgets are destroyed. How user actions return to the Host or Agent while keeping shared-fact boundaries clear. How the same protocol semantics fit both local Agents and remote Agents.
2.title: Core Goals

20.body: Remote/Event binding is used by remote, auditable, event-sourced scenarios such as Robrix2. sequenceDiagram participant A as Remote AgentEndpoint / Producer participant E as Event Log participant H as Host participant R as AppRegistry participant V as View Runtime A->>E: snapshot event with ViewSpec H->>E: read original event content H->>R: lookup AppType + validate version/state R->>V: render registered template with snapshot V-->>H: app card H-->>H: display view Characteristics: The shared event log is the audit source. The Agent/producer is the source of shared truth. The Host is an event consumer, not the Agent's private RPC peer. Shared changes must go through action response, then the Agent sends a new Snapshot. The Host may perform optimistic local view updates, but must not treat optimistic state as shared truth.
20.title: Remote/Event Binding

21.body: Local binding and Remote/Event binding are transport bindings, not business scenarios. aichat uses Local binding; Robrix2 uses Remote/Event binding; future Hosts can use the same kernel with HTTP, WebSocket, or file synchronization.
21.breadcrumbs: Transport Binding » Binding Is Not an Application Scenario
21.title: Binding Is Not an Application Scenario

22.body: Scenario Kernel Binding Profile Focus aichat AppGen Agent2View Core Local Binding LLM-generated UI, local HostState, fast interaction Robrix2 IM Card Agent2View Core Remote/Event Binding Matrix timeline, static templates, plain text fallback Mission Room Agent2View Core Remote/Event Binding room-scoped state, shared actions, human supervision
22.title: Application Scenario Matrix

23.body: Envelope is the concrete encoding of ViewSpec/Snapshot by a Transport Binding. Scope is a protocol-kernel concept and does not belong to any specific transport.
23.breadcrumbs: Envelope and Scope » Envelope and Scope
23.title: Envelope and Scope

24.body:
An Agent2View envelope must express at least: { "type": "mission_room", "core_version": 1, "profile_version": 1, "scope": "room", "app_id": "mission.main", "snapshot": {}, "template_id": "mission_room.v1", "capabilities": {}
} Field semantics: type must match a locally registered AppType. core_version identifies the shared protocol kernel version. profile_version identifies the AppType/profile version. scope defines the identity range of the AppInstance. app_id must be present under room and account scope. snapshot must be a complete state snapshot, not a patch. template_id points to a template allowed by the profile. capabilities declares the state paths, actions, and helpers available to the view. Different bindings may encode these semantics with different field names, but they must not change the semantics.
24.breadcrumbs: Envelope and Scope » Shared Envelope Semantics
24.title: Shared Envelope Semantics

25.body:
Robrix2 / Matrix binding uses the org.octos.app envelope: { "body": "Plain text fallback", "msgtype": "m.text", "org.octos.app": { "type": "mission_room", "version": 1, "scope": "room", "app_id": "mission.main", "initial_state": {} }
} body is required. It is the fallback when rich rendering fails, and it should also summarize the message by itself. The current version is the AppType/profile version. If an explicit core_version is added later, older Hosts can continue to treat version as the compatible profile version.
25.breadcrumbs: Envelope and Scope » Matrix Binding Envelope
25.title: Matrix Binding Envelope

26.body: aichat / Local binding splits the envelope into: appplan json: describes AppType, state paths, actions, and required controls. runsplash: describes Template. HostState: provides the current Snapshot. Together, these three parts are equivalent to the shared ViewSpec. When appplan chooses the A2UI-compatible format, runsplash is no longer a required protocol part. appplan can carry an A2UI createSurface, updateComponents, and updateDataModel message bundle under view.messages. In that case, appplan still owns the Agent2App outer semantics, while A2UI only owns view encoding.
26.breadcrumbs: Envelope and Scope » Local Binding Envelope
26.title: Local Binding Envelope

27.body: flowchart TB S{scope} S --> M[message] S --> R[room] S --> A[account] M --> MK["context_id + message_id/event_id"] R --> RK["context_id/room_id + app_id"] A --> AK["account_id + app_id"]
27.title: ScopeKey

28.body: message scope means one message or response owns an independent app instance. It fits: weather cards; news cards; static information views inside one message; independent demo views in aichat assistant messages.
28.title: Message Scope

29.body: room scope means multiple messages in the same room can point to the same app instance. It fits: mission_room; room-level task boards; room-level agent rosters.
29.title: Room Scope

3.body: flowchart TB Core[Protocol Core Kernel] Core --> Obj[Object model] Core --> State[State model] Core --> Act[Action model] Core --> Val[Validation model] Core --> Bind[Transport Binding] Bind --> Local[Local response / in-process callback] Bind --> Remote[Remote event / action response] Core --> Profile[Application Profile] Profile --> A[aichat] Profile --> R[Robrix2] Profile --> M[Mission Room] The protocol kernel does not care whether the Agent is local or remote, nor whether the transport is an LLM response, Matrix event, HTTP, WebSocket, or a future event system. The kernel defines only stable semantics: AppType, AppInstance, Scope, Snapshot, Template, Action, ActionResult, Capability, and Validation. The transport binding maps those semantics to concrete carriers. For example, aichat puts the view in a runsplash block inside an assistant message; Robrix2 puts the view in an org.octos.app envelope inside a Matrix event. The application profile defines a specific Host's capabilities, restrictions, and UX policy. aichat and Robrix2 are profiles, not two mutually exclusive protocols.
3.title: Layer Boundaries

30.body: account scope means one app instance is shared across rooms under the same account. It fits: mission_dashboard; global agent operations overview. Account scope should not replace room-scoped truth. It can only aggregate state from multiple rooms.
30.title: Account Scope

31.body: If any step fails, the Host must render the safe representation defined by the profile. flowchart TD E[Envelope / ViewSpec] --> P{parse} P -->|fail| B[Fallback] P -->|ok| T{registered AppType} T -->|no| B T -->|yes| V{supported version} V -->|no| B V -->|yes| S{state validates} S -->|no| B S -->|yes| TM{template preflight} TM -->|fail| B TM -->|ok| R[render view]
31.title: Fallback Rules

32.body: Agent2View must distinguish three layers of state. flowchart TB ST[Shared truth<br/>producer snapshot or local authoritative state] HS[Host view state<br/>AgentViewSession / APP_DEMO_STATE] WS[Widget state<br/>focus / hover / animation / IME] ST --> HS HS --> WS WS -. not authoritative .-> HS HS -. local only unless committed .-> ST
32.title: State Model

33.body: Shared truth is a fact that participants can audit, synchronize, or reproduce. In a remote/event binding, shared truth must come from a producer snapshot, such as the original content of a Matrix event. In a local binding, shared truth can temporarily be held by HostState, such as aichat's APP_DEMO_STATE. Even then, widget state must not become shared truth. Shared state changes must go through AppType policy. Remote scenarios must use a new snapshot event sent by an Agent/producer; local scenarios can update the local snapshot through a Host reducer.
33.title: Shared Truth

34.body: Host view state is the local state kept by the Host for rendering and interaction. It is used to: withstand widget destruction caused by PortalList virtualization; support local UI reducers; re-render visible views that point to the same room/account scoped instance; store volatile input, selection, filters, expanded/collapsed flags, and other UI state. Robrix2 v1 may keep Host view state only in memory. Persistence is future work.
34.title: Host View State

35.body: Widget state can only be temporary rendering state, for example: IME composition; hover/focus; scroll offset; animation progress. Widget state must not become the authoritative state of an AppInstance.
35.title: Widget State

36.body: For room and account scoped apps, producer events should provide complete snapshots. stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> NoSession NoSession --> CleanSession: first valid snapshot CleanSession --> DirtySession: local reducer DirtySession --> DirtySession: redraw same event DirtySession --> CleanSession: newer producer snapshot CleanSession --> CleanSession: newer producer snapshot CleanSession --> CleanSession: old event redraw ignored Projection rules: A newer valid snapshot replaces session shared state. Redrawing an older timeline item must not roll the session back. Repeated redraw of the same event must not clear local dirty reducer state. When a new producer snapshot arrives, dirty is cleared because shared truth has advanced.
36.title: Snapshot Projection

37.body: Draft state in an input field belongs to Host view state, not Template source. In aichat, {{state.input.*.value}} should not be replaced with new source on every display render; otherwise every character would trigger Markdown/Splash set_text and rebuild the UI. The correct model is: TextInput writes draft text into HostState. Template remains stable. Add/Submit actions read draft text from HostState. The rendering layer projects display values only when needed.
37.title: Volatile Input

38.body: The protocol kernel only defines Template semantics: Template projects Snapshot/HostState into UI and exposes whitelisted Actions. The Template source is decided by the profile. The Template encoding is also decided by the profile. Current encodings include Makepad runsplash and A2UI component trees. } During display rendering, the Host should treat {{state.input.*.value}} as a volatile placeholder. Shared Fact Action changes shared facts. It must be validated by the Agent/producer and then produce a new Snapshot. Examples in Mission Room: approve_plan

47.body:
aichat uses agent.notify(event_id, payload) to carry Action: agent.notify("inc", {})
agent.notify("app.collection.add_from_input", {collection: "items", input: "new_item"}) agent.notify is the reverse channel of the aichat Local Binding. It is not the shared protocol kernel itself; it is the local carrier that maps user intent inside a Template back to the Host action dispatcher. Implementation boundary: agent.notify is registered in widgets/src/splash.rs. SplashAction is defined in widgets/src/splash.rs. SplashAction::Notify is a bare action, not a widget action. aichat directly iterates actions and casts in handle_actions. Call contract: The first argument is event_id. It must be convertible to a string; a missing or invalid value becomes an empty string. The second argument is payload. It can be any Splash value, and the runtime serializes it into a JSON string. agent.notify does not return a business value. It returns nil. It can be used inside generated runsplash callbacks such as Button.on_click and TextInput.on_change. Runtime path: sequenceDiagram participant UI as runsplash UI participant VM as Splash VM participant CX as Cx action queue participant H as aichat Host participant S as Host data/state UI->>VM: agent.notify(event_id, payload) VM->>VM: stringify event_id and JSON-encode payload VM->>CX: Cx::post_action(SplashAction::Notify) CX->>H: handle_actions H->>H: whitelist event_id and validate payload H->>S: mutate local data/state or trigger agent callback H->>UI: refresh visible templates The Host must: validate event id; validate payload JSON; log and ignore unknown events; log and ignore invalid payloads. State refresh rules: The Host is the data/state owner. runsplash is only the current view template. After a valid action changes Host data/state, the Host projects the current data/state back into the visible template. Draft state in input fields must not rewrite the runsplash source on every keypress. Input should call agent.notify("app.input.set", ...) into HostState, and a submit action should consume it. Boundary: agent.notify can carry local_view actions and aichat-local agent_callback actions. It must not be used as the production protocol for remote shared fact actions in scenarios such as Robrix2. Remote shared actions should use the corresponding transport binding, such as org.octos.action_response in Matrix.
47.title: Local Binding: agent.notify

48.body:
Robrix2 uses org.octos.action_response to carry Shared Fact Action. { "org.octos.action_response": { "action_id": "approve_plan", "source_event_id": "$mission123", "app": { "type": "mission_room", "version": 1, "scope": "room", "app_id": "mission.main" } }
} Rules: source_event_id points to the original Matrix event that produced the action. The app field explicitly routes the action when multiple app instances exist in the same room. The producer validates the action response. After applying policy, the producer sends a new app snapshot event. Robrix2 may perform optimistic local view updates, but must not treat optimistic state as shared truth.
48.title: Remote Binding: action_response

49.body: A2UI can serve as the Agent2App View Encoding. It does not replace the Agent2App Core Kernel. Agent2App defines app-instance semantics: AppType, Scope, Snapshot, Action, Capability, Validation, and application profiles. A2UI defines streamable UI representation: Surface, Component, Data Model, and user action. The compatibility strategy is: Agent2App appplan = Agent2App outer semantics + A2UI message bundle Do not put Agent2App fields such as scope, app_type, profile policy, or permission boundaries directly inside A2UI messages. The A2UI v0.9 server-to-client envelope is a strict message structure; each message can express only one A2UI operation.

52.body: A2UI v0.9 server-to-client messages include: createSurface: creates a renderable surface. updateComponents: updates the component list of that surface. updateDataModel: updates the data model of that surface. deleteSurface: deletes the surface. Recommended Agent2App to A2UI mapping: Agent2App Concept A2UI Concept Notes app_id surfaceId message scope may be assigned by the Host; room/account scope should use a stable app id. Snapshot updateDataModel.value Prefer committing the full snapshot at /; partial patches fit only bindings with strong ordering guarantees. Template / ViewSpec updateComponents.components Use the A2UI component catalog for a validated UI structure. CapabilityManifest catalogId + client capabilities A2UI catalog expresses component/function capability; Agent2App manifest still expresses state/action permissions. Local View Action action.functionCall Use only for Host-registered local functions such as openUrl. Shared Fact Action action.event Send to the Host/Agent for validation, then produce a new Snapshot. ActionResult new envelope after client-to-server action An A2UI action itself is not shared truth; truth still converges through Agent2App Snapshot.

53.body:
When appplan is A2UI-compatible, it is still an Agent2App artifact, not a single A2UI message. Recommended format: { "agent2app": { "core_version": 1, "binding_version": 1, "profile": "aichat", "profile_version": 1, "app_type": "todo", "scope": "message", "app_id": "todo.main" }, "view": { "format": "a2ui", "version": "v0.9", "messages": [ { "version": "v0.9", "createSurface": { "surfaceId": "todo.main", "catalogId": "https://a2ui.org/specification/v0_9/standard_catalog.json", "sendDataModel": true } }, { "version": "v0.9", "updateComponents": { "surfaceId": "todo.main", "components": [ { "id": "root", "component": "Column", "children": ["new_item", "add_button", "items"] }, { "id": "new_item", "component": "TextField", "label": "New item", "value": { "path": "/inputs/new_item/value" }, "variant": "shortText" }, { "id": "add_button_label", "component": "Text", "text": "Add" }, { "id": "add_button", "component": "Button", "child": "add_button_label", "variant": "primary", "action": { "event": { "name": "app.collection.add_from_input", "context": { "collection": "items", "input": "new_item" } } } }, { "id": "items", "component": "List", "children": { "path": "/collections/items/rows", "componentId": "item_template" } }, { "id": "item_template", "component": "Text", "text": { "path": "text" } } ] } }, { "version": "v0.9", "updateDataModel": { "surfaceId": "todo.main", "path": "/", "value": { "inputs": { "new_item": { "value": "" } }, "collections": { "items": { "rows": [] } } } } } ] }, "permissions": { "state_paths": [ "/inputs/new_item/value", "/collections/items/rows" ], "actions": [ "app.collection.add_from_input" ] }
} This structure has two important boundaries: view.messages[*] must be valid A2UI v0.9 messages. agent2app and permissions are Agent2App outer semantics; an A2UI renderer is not required to understand them natively.

54.body: A2UI input components use local two-way binding: TextField, CheckBox, Slider, ChoicePicker, and similar components immediately update the client-side data model when the user interacts with them. 87.title: Fail Closed to Safe Rendering

88.body: Agent2App versioning has three layers: core version, binding version, and AppType/profile version.
88.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation
88.title: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation

89.body: core_version describes the protocol kernel version. It controls: object model; ScopeKey semantics; Snapshot semantics; Action / ActionResult semantics; CapabilityManifest semantics; shared validation order. Local Agents and remote Agents must use consistent core version semantics.
89.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » Core Version
89.title: Core Version

9.body: AgentEndpoint represents the Agent endpoint that produces an app view or handles a shared action. It can be: a local LLM session; a local tool Agent; a remote Agent in a Matrix room; a server-side producer. The location of the AgentEndpoint does not change the protocol object model. Remote Agents and local Agents both produce the same semantic ViewSpec, Snapshot, and Action.
9.title: AgentEndpoint

90.body: binding_version describes the transport mapping version. For example: how aichat local binding encodes appplan json, runsplash, and agent.notify; how Robrix2 Matrix binding encodes org.octos.app and org.octos.action_response. Binding version changes should not change core semantics. They should only change carrier format or transport-specific metadata. When a binding carries A2UI, it should also declare a view encoding version, for example view.format = "a2ui" and view.version = "v0.9". A2UI version changes affect only view encoding and should not change Agent2App Scope, Snapshot, or ActionResult semantics.
90.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » Binding Version
90.title: Binding Version

91.body: version is the AppType or profile-level protocol version. It controls: concrete state schema; concrete template id; concrete action set; concrete profile policy. The Host may support multiple versions. Unsupported versions must fall back.
91.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » AppType / Scenario Version
91.title: AppType / Scenario Version

92.body: When adding optional fields, older Hosts may ignore them. When changing the semantics of an existing field, the relevant version must be bumped. Version bump rules: Change shared object semantics: bump core version. Change transport encoding: bump binding version. Change a specific AppType state/action/template semantic: bump AppType/profile version.
92.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » Field Compatibility
92.title: Field Compatibility

93.body: State schema should define: required fields; optional fields; default values; enum values; maximum array lengths or render truncation rules. The Mission Room v1 template may limit visible counts, for example: first 6 tasks; first 4 agents; first 3 pending actions.
93.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » State Compatibility
93.title: State Compatibility

94.body:
Non-UI validation: cargo check -p makepad-example-aichat --release
cargo test -p makepad-example-aichat --release input
cargo test -p makepad-example-aichat --release collection UI validation must use a Studio remote release run. A raw cargo run is not accepted as UI validation.
94.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » aichat Validation
94.title: aichat Validation

95.body: Robrix2 v1 validation: valid org.octos.app envelope renders a static Splash card; invalid envelope falls back to body; unknown AppType falls back; unsupported version falls back; unsafe template fails preflight; message scope is isolated by room_id + event_id; room scope is shared by room_id + app_id; mission room event uses room_id + mission.main as the instance key; shared action sends org.octos.action_response and does not directly rewrite shared truth.
95.breadcrumbs: Versioning, Compatibility, and Validation » Robrix2 Validation
95.title: Robrix2 Validation

96.breadcrumbs: Non-Goals and Roadmap » Non-Goals and Roadmap
96.title: Non-Goals and Roadmap

97.body: This v0.1 specification does not include: Agent2Project artifact manifest; running LLM-generated templates in the Robrix2 production path; plugin marketplace; dynamic capability discovery; automatic repair loop; multi-Agent resolver/template-author division-of-labor protocol; client persistence for room/account scoped state; full recursive subtask/project-management model.
97.title: Non-Goals

98.body: Possible future protocols: Agent2Project artifact protocol; Robrix2 L2 action-capable cards; Robrix2 L3 stateful runtime; generated template opt-in profile; capability discovery protocol; Mission dashboard account scope profile; multi-mission room routing rules. These extensions should each have their own spec. They should not be pushed into the v0.1 Agent2View core protocol. flowchart LR V01[v0.1 Agent2View core] V01 --> L2[Robrix2 L2 actions] V01 --> L3[Robrix2 L3 stateful runtime] V01 --> GP[Generated template opt-in] V01 --> AP[Agent2Project artifact protocol] V01 --> MD[Mission dashboard account profile]
98.title: Future Extensions
